value.overview: The Ocellated Crake is a small, secretive rail of tropical grasslands and savannas. It spends most of its time walking through dense vegetation, where its mottled cinnamon, black, and white plumage provides effective camouflage. Although widespread in parts of Central and South America, it has a scattered distribution and is seldom seen. In Costa Rica it is a rare, highly local bird, best detected by its distinctive calls rather than by direct observation.
value.classification: The Ocellated Crake belongs to the rail family, Rallidae, in the order Gruiformes. It is currently placed in the genus Rufirallus; older references may use the name Micropygia schomburgkii.
value.identification: This small crake has warm cinnamon or rufous coloration on the face, breast, and underparts, with conspicuous black-and-white spotting and barring on the upperparts, wings, and flanks. Its short tail, rounded body, and secretive ground-dwelling habits are typical of crakes. It is more often heard than seen. The song is a distinctive solitary trill, while alarm calls can sound like a rapid, sizzling or whirring series of notes, especially around dawn and dusk.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a scattered range from southern Costa Rica through Panama and northern South America, with separate populations extending across the Guianas, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Paraguay, and Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a rare and very local resident, reported particularly in southern Puntarenas, including the Ujarrás and Salitre area. It uses tall, dense grasslands, marshy savannas, seasonally flooded pastures, and grassy wetland margins, generally in lowlands and away from closed forest.
value.migrationStatus: It is regarded as a non-migratory resident. In Costa Rica, the species is present year-round where suitable habitat remains, although local movements may occur as water levels, grass growth, and burning alter its grassland habitat.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited because the species is difficult to observe. It is believed to form monogamous pairs and build a domed nest from dry grasses, with a side or covered entrance concealed in dense vegetation. The female is reported to incubate the eggs. In Costa Rica, breeding is suspected mainly during the rainy season, approximately May through November, but detailed information on nesting sites, clutch size, and chick development remains scarce.
value.dietFeeding: The Ocellated Crake forages on the ground beneath tall grass and other dense vegetation. Its diet is chiefly made up of insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, grasshoppers, cockroaches, ants, and related prey. It searches by walking slowly through cover and probing among stems, leaf litter, and damp ground. Feeding activity is difficult to observe because the bird usually remains hidden.
value.behavior: This crake is shy, elusive, and strongly associated with dense ground cover. It usually walks rather than flies, but may make a short, low flight when flushed. Individuals are most vocal around dawn and dusk, when their trills carry across open grasslands. The species can occupy both wet and relatively dry grasslands, particularly where vegetation is tall and dense after natural or human-caused disturbance such as seasonal fire.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is suspected to be declining, although reliable population estimates and long-term monitoring are lacking. In Costa Rica, it is rare and local, so changes in a few grassland areas could have a disproportionate effect on the national population.
conservation.threats: The main concerns are loss and degradation of tall grassland, marsh, and savanna through drainage, conversion to agriculture or development, intensive grazing, and inappropriate fire management. Because the species depends on dense cover, repeated burning, mowing, or clearing during the breeding season may reduce nesting and feeding habitat. Its rarity in Costa Rica also makes it vulnerable to the loss of small, isolated sites.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining lowland grasslands, marshes, and seasonally flooded savannas in southern Costa Rica, especially known sites in Puntarenas. Maintain a varied mosaic of tall grass and open areas rather than clearing or burning entire sites at once, and avoid mowing or intensive burning during the likely rainy-season breeding period. Reporting sightings, calls, and habitat conditions to established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this poorly documented species.
